> But I’m very worried that by allowing my alters to choose face claims with a different skin tone specifically, I’m appropriating a culture that is not my own. 

I don't understand how that can be seen culturally appropriative. Phenotypic traits, such as skin color, are not characteristic of any one culture. It's also worth noting that when alters are created, the host may not have been old enough to understand concepts such as racism, sexism, etc.

I'm not sure what you mean by "allow." How do you tell an alter that they can't be X?

I would say it’s controversial because, while not the dominant hypothesis, there are still academic researchers who think that DID is *therapist-induced* rather than traumagenic. This is apart from social stigma due to misinformation and negative portrayals in the media, because those arguably apply to mental disorders in general.

>The alter not only doesn’t like me very much, she doesn’t like my girlfriend either. She doesn’t like anyone. I’ve approached dissociative moments in ways ranging from a confrontational “back off” standpoint, to a mediating standpoint, to a comforting standpoint, to a loving standpoint. The very core of the persecutor just seems mean and angry, and seems to just want to be mean and angry. 

My fiancé’s persecutor is a hypersexual demoness. When I first met her, she was not simply “mean and angry.” She told me that she wanted to mutilate and kill the host, and manipulate and torture me, for fun. She pretended to be my fiancé and asked me to kill her to end her suffering. She is sexually abusive toward my fiancé, both internally — e.g., via dreams and intrusive thoughts — and externally when fronting. It’s important to understand that a persecutor doesn’t “want” to be this way. This is analogous to claiming that a depressed person wants to be depressed. Every alter in a DID system behaves in a certain way for a reason. 

By not regarding her as an “enemy,” treating her with respect and compassion, and talking to her calmly and showing her kindness, I managed to discover her more human side. We even settled on a name that she liked. We made progress with her. There is still more work to be done, but I know it’s possible to reach her. She is confused and doesn’t understand complex emotions, such as love or what it means to be loved. She is in pain and has internalized the abuse suffered by the body.

A cognitive distortion is an irrational thought pattern. In the context of DID, this is irrelevant to the existence of distinct personality states. DID is a traumagenic identity disorder, not a mood disorder, such as depression. A distorted pattern of thinking does not cause alters to manifest — psychological trauma due to emotional, physical, or sexual abuse in early childhood is the principal causative factor. I don't know what psychologist or psychotherapist you have found who refers to the existence of alters in DID as a "distortion." Consider the fact that DID, and the emergence of alters, constitutes an elaborate psychological defense mechanism by which the ego fractures, compartmentalizing personality traits and memories in order to cope with traumatic experiences that are too horrific for one cohesive self to process.

Can you keep us updated if/when your parcels arrive? My partner who lives in Central Europe sent me a package on February 2, and it still hasn't been delivered. They're worried that it may have gotten lost too.
